subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If n is a positive integer and x is any non-zero real number, then prove that C₀ + C₁·(x/2) + C₂·(x²/3) + C₃·(x³/4) + … + Cₙ·(xⁿ/(n + 1)) = ((1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/((n + 1)x).

mark_split.label: Multiply by x, then by n + 1

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — what you multiply the sum by and why, which identity raises the index to n + 1, what the new sum adds up to, and how you divide back to get S.
insider_note: Two multiplications, in order: by x so the powers match the denominators, then by n + 1. At the end divide by (n + 1)x — dividing by n + 1 alone leaves the x and loses the final mark.

steps.label: Write the sum with ⁿCᵣ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Cᵣ means ⁿCᵣ. The denominators run 1, 2, 3, …, n + 1 — one more than the index every time.
steps.memory_tip: Cᵣ means ⁿCᵣ, and the denominators run one ahead of the index: 1, 2, 3, …, n + 1.

recall.must_convey: That the sum is named S and each Cᵣ is written as ⁿCᵣ with denominator r + 1.
accept: let S be the sum and write each C r as n C r with the denominator r plus one
S equals n C nought plus n C one x by two plus n C two x squared by three and so on

steps.why: Naming the left side S and writing Cᵣ as ⁿCᵣ makes the index n visible, and n is what the next step changes into n + 1.
common_mistakes: Reading the denominators as r instead of r + 1.
Dropping the x from the terms.

steps.label: Multiply by x, then by n + 1
steps.margin_note: Second and third marks. Multiplying by x raises every power by one so it matches the denominator; multiplying by n + 1 puts (n + 1)/(r + 1) in front of each ⁿCᵣ.
steps.memory_tip: TWO multiplications: by x to lift each power to match its denominator, then by n + 1.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying S by x and then by n + 1 gives terms ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ·xʳ⁺¹.
accept: multiply by x so the powers match the denominators then by n plus one so each term has n plus one by r plus one in front
n plus one x S equals n plus one by one n C nought x plus n plus one by two n C one x squared and so on
multiply both sides by n plus one times x
x tho, tarvata n plus one tho multiply cheste prathi term lo n plus one by r plus one vasthundi
the factor n plus one over r plus one appears in every term
heard_as: n plus one by r plus one

steps.why: The denominators 1, 2, 3, …, n + 1 are the r + 1 in ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ. Multiplying by n + 1 makes each term exactly that identity.
common_mistakes: Multiplying by n + 1 alone and leaving the powers one short of the denominators.

steps.label: Use ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁ — one row down, one index along. Every term of the sum becomes a coefficient of (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹.
steps.memory_tip: ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁. The sum becomes (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ with its first term missing.

recall.must_convey: That each ((n + 1)/(r + 1))·ⁿCᵣ becomes ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁, so (n + 1)xS = ⁿ⁺¹C₁x + ⁿ⁺¹C₂x² + … + ⁿ⁺¹Cₙ₊₁xⁿ⁺¹.
accept: n plus one by r plus one times n C r is n plus one C r plus one so the sum becomes n plus one C one x plus n plus one C two x squared and so on

each term becomes a coefficient of one plus x to the n plus one

n plus one by r plus one

steps.why: Once every term is ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁ times a power of x, the whole sum is the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ with its first term missing.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the sum now starts at ⁿ⁺¹C₁, not ⁿ⁺¹C₀.

steps.label: Sum the expansion and divide
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. The new sum is (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ without its leading 1. Divide by (n + 1)x.
steps.memory_tip: The missing term is ⁿ⁺¹C₀ = 1, so subtract it. Then divide by (n + 1)x — both factors, not just n + 1.

recall.must_convey: That the sum equals (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ − 1, so S = ((1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/((n + 1)x).
accept: the sum is one plus x to the n plus one minus one, divide by n plus one x to get S
n plus one x S equals one plus x to the n plus one minus one
S equals one plus x to the n plus one minus one over n plus one x

the expansion without its first term is one plus x to the n plus one minus one
heard_as: one plus x to the n plus one

steps.why: ⁿ⁺¹C₁x + ⁿ⁺¹C₂x² + … + ⁿ⁺¹Cₙ₊₁xⁿ⁺¹ is (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ minus its first term 1. Dividing back by what was multiplied gives S.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the −1: the term ⁿ⁺¹C₀ = 1 is not in the sum.
Dividing by n + 1 only and leaving the x.
